A close reading for the week

“The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne”

Antony and Cleopatra · Act 2, Scene 2

The most sumptuous description in Shakespeare is spoken in Rome, by a soldier, to two men who have never seen her. Cleopatra is never more present than when she is being reported.

EnobarbusI will tell you.
The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne,
Burned on the water.1 The poop was beaten gold;
Purple the sails, and so perfumed that
The winds were love-sick with them;2 the oars were silver,

  1. 1

    Fire on water

    The barge “burned on the water”, gold so bright it seems to set the river alight. Shakespeare took the scene from Plutarch (in North’s translation), where the barge has a poop of gold and purple sails but does not burn; the burning is his. The first image fuses the elements that should not mix, and the whole speech follows: winds in love, water chasing oars, air that would leave its place. Cleopatra disorders nature by being looked at.

  2. 2

    Everything falls in love

    The sails are so perfumed that “the winds were love-sick with them”; the water, beaten by the oars, follows faster “as amorous of their strokes”. Enobarbus makes the physical world Cleopatra’s first set of lovers. The conceit is extravagant and exact: a boat moving upstream, wind in the sails, the wake behind, every ordinary fact of sailing recast as desire.
